examples.question_text: A curve passes through the origin and has gradient function $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4x^{3}-6x$. Find its equation.
Given $f'(x)=3x^{2}+2x-1$ and $f(-1)=4$, find $f(2)$ and the $y$-intercept of its graph.
Given $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sqrt{x}$ and $y=7$ when $x=9$, find $y$ in terms of $x$.
examples.solution_text:
Write the square root as a fractional power.
$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=x^{\frac12}\\y&=\dfrac{x^{\frac32}}{\frac32}+C\\&=\dfrac23x^{\frac32}+C\end{align*}$
Substitute $(9,7)$.
$\begin{align*}7&=\dfrac23(9)^{\frac32}+C\\7&=18+C\\C&=-11\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}y&=\dfrac23x^{\frac32}-11\end{align*}$

Rewrite the reciprocal term using a negative power.
$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=2x^{3}-6x^{-2}\\f(x)&=\dfrac{2x^{4}}4-\dfrac{6x^{-1}}{-1}+C\\&=\dfrac{x^{4}}2+\dfrac6x+C\end{align*}$
Substitute $f(1)=8$.
$\begin{align*}8&=\dfrac{1^{4}}2+\dfrac61+C\\8&=\dfrac{13}2+C\\C&=\dfrac32\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\dfrac{x^{4}}2+\dfrac6x+\dfrac32\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Given $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(3x-2)^{3}$ and $y=2$ when $x=1$, find $y$ in terms of $x$.
examples.solution_text:
Increase the power by one and divide by the new power and the coefficient of $x$.
$\begin{align*}y&=\dfrac{(3x-2)^{4}}{3(4)}+C\\&=\dfrac{(3x-2)^{4}}{12}+C\end{align*}$
Substitute $(1,2)$.
$\begin{align*}2&=\dfrac{(3(1)-2)^{4}}{12}+C\\2&=\dfrac1{12}+C\\C&=\dfrac{23}{12}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}y&=\dfrac{(3x-2)^{4}}{12}+\dfrac{23}{12}\end{align*}$

Expand before finding the primitive.
$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=(x+2)(x-2)\\&=x^{2}-4\\f(x)&=\dfrac{x^{3}}3-4x+C\end{align*}$
Substitute $f(3)=7$.
$\begin{align*}7&=\dfrac{3^{3}}3-4(3)+C\\7&=-3+C\\C&=10\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\dfrac{x^{3}}3-4x+10\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A function has $f''(x)=12x+6$, $f'(1)=8$ and $f(1)=3$. Find $f(x)$ and hence $f(2)$.
examples.solution_text:
Find the first primitive and use the gradient condition.
$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=6x^{2}+6x+C_{1}\\8&=6(1)^{2}+6(1)+C_{1}\\8&=12+C_{1}\\C_{1}&=-4\\f'(x)&=6x^{2}+6x-4\end{align*}$
Find the second primitive and use the point condition.
$\begin{align*}f(x)&=2x^{3}+3x^{2}-4x+C_{2}\\3&=2(1)^{3}+3(1)^{2}-4(1)+C_{2}\\3&=1+C_{2}\\C_{2}&=2\\f(x)&=2x^{3}+3x^{2}-4x+2\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}f(2)&=2(2)^{3}+3(2)^{2}-4(2)+2\\&=22\end{align*}$

Practice and quiz mathematics remain unchanged and were not re-audited. examples.derivation: Integrating gives f(x)=2x^3-2x^2+C. At x=2, 5=8+C, so C=-3. Differentiating the final function gives 6x^2-4x, and f(2)=5.
Integrating gives y=x^4-3x^2+C. The origin gives C=0. The final derivative is 4x^3-6x and y(0)=0.
The primitive is f(x)=x^3+x^2-x+C. At x=-1 its nonconstant terms total 1, giving C=3. Thus f(2)=8+4-2+3=13 and the y-intercept is (0,3). Differentiation recovers the given derivative.
The primitive of x^(1/2) is (2/3)x^(3/2)+C. Since 9^(3/2)=27, 7=18+C gives C=-11. The final function has derivative sqrt(x) and value 7 at x=9.
Integrating 2x^3-6x^(-2) gives x^4/2+6/x+C. At x=1, 8=13/2+C, so C=3/2. Differentiation gives 2x^3-6/x^2. The stated domain x>0 contains the initial point and avoids the singularity.
The linear-power rule gives y=(3x-2)^4/12+C. Substituting (1,2) gives C=23/12. Differentiation gives (3x-2)^3, and y(1)=2.
Integrating (2x+1)^(1/2) gives (2x+1)^(3/2)/3+C. At x=4, the primitive term is 27/3=9, so C=-4. Differentiation recovers sqrt(2x+1), and f(4)=5.
Expansion gives (x+2)(x-2)=x^2-4. Its primitive is x^3/3-4x+C. At x=3, 7=-3+C gives C=10. The final derivative is x^2-4 and f(3)=7.

First integration gives f'(x)=6x^2+6x+C1; f'(1)=8 gives C1=-4. Second integration gives f(x)=2x^3+3x^2-4x+C2; f(1)=3 gives C2=2. Therefore f(2)=16+12-8+2=22. Both initial conditions and f''(x)=12x+6 are satisfied.
